# spine: do the pilot's own six months make the case for a townwide program, or against it?
[S1] The pilot ran six months in the Kettle Row district and pulled sixty-three tons of food waste out of the landfill. At the county tipping fee, that saved the town two thousand three hundred ninety-four dollars.
[S2] Hold on. Running it cost fifteen thousand two hundred forty-four dollars over those same six months. The landfill savings cover about a sixth of that. Six months in and the ledger is upside down.
[S1] Start at the beginning. Brayling Public Works ran this in the Kettle Row district from March second to September first. The council signed off in November of twenty twenty-five, after an R F P for hauling drew three bids.
[S2] Four hundred twelve households out of six hundred forty invited. Sixty-four percent sign-up is strong for a curbside program... and a volunteer group is the easy half of any town.
[S1] The tipping fee is the part worth holding onto. Thirty-eight dollars a ton is what the county charges to bury it, so every ton the carts caught was thirty-eight dollars the town kept.
[S2] Which is a real number and a small one. You would expect the landfill savings to carry a program like this. Sixty-three tons at thirty-eight dollars a ton does not come close to what it cost.
[S1] Marta Vinh, the coordinator, puts the per household cost at seventy-four dollars a year. Her point in the report is that the number does not fall much as the program gets bigger.
[S2] That is the claim I want tested, and the report does not test it. It never estimates what a townwide program would cost. Seventy-four dollars a household is a pilot's number carried forward on faith.
[S1] Participation held up better than I expected. Sixty-eight percent of enrolled households set a cart out in a typical week, which for a voluntary program asking people to keep scraps in a pail is a lot.
[S2] Until July. It dropped to fifty-one percent in July, and the department logged thirty-seven odor complaints across the whole pilot... twenty-nine of them in that one month. Heat found the flaw.
[S1] Contamination went the other way. Plastic bags and produce stickers were eleven percent of the first sampled load by weight. By the sixth month it was four percent, after a second mailer and stickers for the cart lids.
[S2] Okay, that one I believe, and it is the cheapest thing in the report. Two mailers and a sheet of stickers cut contamination by more than half. Nobody is going to put that on a slide.
[S1] Here is the number Ellis Trant leans on. Total M S W tonnage out of Kettle Row fell twelve percent against the same six months of twenty twenty-five. That is the district throwing away less.
[S2] Part of it. The district also lost eighteen households to vacancy over that stretch, and empty houses throw away nothing at all. The report says as much, and then leans on the twelve percent anyway.
[S1] Trant's recommendation is a second six months rather than an expansion. The case for the program, in that reading, rests on the twelve percent and on what the windrow site actually yields as compost.
[S2] And that yield is the second thing the report never measures. It cannot say whether the windrow site could take a townwide volume, and it cannot say what a townwide program would cost. Two holes.
[S1] So here is where I land. Six months bought Brayling a working collection route, a contamination rate under control, and no idea what the thing costs at scale. Extend it. The council votes in October.
[S2] I land close to that. The pilot made its case on twelve percent and a clean sorted load, and it never made the money case at all. Six more months should be spent costing the rollout.
